items.summary: `PYPTO_BENCH=1` times post-graph-build device execution after a correctness dispatch. Compare the printed `mean` field with identical warmup and rounds; distributed runs add per-rank and per-dispatch slots, where the headline is the slowest rank per round.
items.text: `PYPTO_BENCH=1` enables a timed loop on every `run` call after the correctness dispatch. No `--benchmark` flag or model edit is needed. The printed `effective_us` is the framework's post-graph-build execution window on device, recovered from runtime markers. Quote the `mean=` field for a generic Golden per-case comparison; two runs are comparable only when both use the same warmup and measured round counts. `PYPTO_BENCH_ROUNDS` defaults to 100 and `PYPTO_BENCH_WARMUP` to 5; `PYPTO_BENCH_RAW=1` prints every measured dispatch sample in dispatch order. A malformed or out-of-range value warns and falls back to the default. The benchmark requires a real device; simulator platforms print `effective_us unavailable: no device-domain spans`. It also requires a runtime built with profiling support. A `runtime_dir=` replay times an existing build without recompiling; a spec with a stepped scalar skips the benchmark. In a distributed run the headline is the per-round maximum across ranks because the round ends when the slowest card finishes. The `rank N: eff_us` lines expose cross-card imbalance and sum that card's dispatches within a round. When a card dispatches more than once per round, nested `slot` lines show each dispatch's window and the orchestration function name; slot lines may be omitted when every card dispatches once or when dispatch order varies between rounds. `host_union_mean_us` is the cross-rank host-timeline window `max(end) - min(start)`, so it includes start skew, overlap, and host dispatch overhead. `fallback_flattened=1` means the dispatch count was not divisible by warmup plus rounds, so per-round segmentation was abandoned and the numbers are indicative pooled samples. The benchmark replays the same weights every round, so L2 is already warm; a change whose benefit depends on a cold cache is both flattered and diluted, and production numbers should come from an unprofiled benchmark. A source change needs an end-to-end before/after number rather than a kernel-level guess. A distributed program shows a persistent per-rank imbalance. A change affects L2 weight residency and the benchmark's warm-cache replay would flatter it. Run `PYPTO_BENCH=1 python models/.../entry.py -p <platform> -d <device>` and compare the `mean=` field for the generic Golden harness, not `min`, `median`, or a profile capture. While iterating on a long prefill, reduce `PYPTO_BENCH_ROUNDS` and `PYPTO_BENCH_WARMUP` together, but compare only against runs with the same settings. When only timing changes, save the golden once and replay with `golden_data=` to avoid recomputing the torch reference. For a multi-dispatch distributed card, read the `slot` breakdown to identify which dispatch owns the time; do not infer it from the rank total. A simulator platform has no device-domain spans and cannot produce `effective_us`. The runtime must be built with profiling support. A stepped scalar skips the timed loop. The benchmark is an execution measurement, not a source-level correctness check; retain numerical validation separately. A warm-cache replay does not represent cold-cache production behavior for L2-residency changes. The generic Golden harness uses `mean=`; benchmark harness clean evaluation uses `median_effective_us` and profile-fixed rounds. Do not mix conventions. Repeated rounds reduce noise but multiply compile/input/golden cost and device time. A full 100-round default is comparable across runs but costly for a long prefill; shortened loops are faster but only comparable within the same settings. Level-4 chip-swimlane capture gives causal detail but has observer cost; use it for causality and the unprofiled benchmark for the production number. items.summary: `pl.set_cache_policy(tensor, pl.CachePolicy.BYPASS)` declares every read of a tensor in a scope streaming; `pl.load(..., cache=...)` declares one access. BYPASS is a coherence and no-reuse contract, not a hint. The installed toolchain has no L2-bypass path yet, so it warns and compiles as an ordinary cached access.
items.text: The scope-level cache surface is `pl.set_cache_policy(tensor, policy)`, written as a standalone statement directly inside a `pl.at(level=pl.Level.CORE_GROUP, ...)` or `pl.spmd(...)` body. It covers every read of that tensor in the scope, including implicit reads inside `pl.matmul`, `pl.assemble`, and subscript slicing. The per-access counterpart is `pl.load(..., cache=pl.CachePolicy.BYPASS)`; `pl.slice` deliberately takes no `cache=` because it computes an address descriptor rather than moving data. An explicit load policy always wins over a scope declaration in both directions, so `cache=pl.CachePolicy.DEFAULT` can opt one read back into the cache inside a bypassing scope. `CachePolicy.BYPASS` asserts two things: the bytes have no reuse worth caching, and nothing writes those bytes while the kernel runs. Mixing a cached write with a bypassing read is a coherency bug the compiler cannot detect. Declaring BYPASS on a tensor the scope itself writes is rejected at outlining. The declaration is tracked by Var identity, not name; rebinding the tensor after the declaration produces a new value the declaration does not cover. A declaration on a non-`CORE_GROUP` `pl.at` scope is parsed and carried but not lowered, so it has no effect. Current status: PTOAS has no L2-bypass path yet. A BYPASS request is accepted, warns at compile time, and generates exactly the same code as an ordinary cached access. Writing it now costs nothing and starts working when the path lands. For weight residency, `pl.prefetch` is the documented module-level cache-warm surface: it writes no tensor and is free to try and delete, but a partial or oversized warm can cost more than it saves. The benchmark loop replays the same weights every round, so its L2 is already warm; a prefetch or cold-cache change is both flattered and diluted by that replay. The corpus does not expose the concrete `pl.prefetch` method signatures in its registered API extracts, so do not invent them. A weight matrix is read once per stage and evicts a smaller activation set that is reread. A stage re-reads a fixed weight set every layer after a large unrelated stage has evicted it. A benchmark replays the same weights every round and overstates a warm-cache benefit. Add `pl.set_cache_policy(weights, pl.CachePolicy.BYPASS)` as a standalone statement inside the `pl.at` or `pl.spmd` body that reads the weights. For a tile-level load whose policy is local, use `pl.load(weights, [n0, k0], [N_TILE, K_TILE], cache=pl.CachePolicy.BYPASS)`. Use `pl.prefetch` only after checking the installed method surface and only where a fixed weight set is re-read after an eviction; measure with an unprofiled benchmark that does not replay a permanently warm cache. Do not combine a bypassing read with a cached write of the same bytes. BYPASS is a correctness contract about no reuse and no concurrent writer, not merely a performance preference. A scope declaration must be directly inside the scope body; nesting it in an `if` or `for` inside the scope is rejected. Only a `CORE_GROUP` `pl.at` or `pl.spmd` scope lowers the declaration; other levels carry it without effect. The compiler rejects BYPASS on a tensor the scope writes, but cannot prove the general no-writer case. The current PTOAS path emits the same code for BYPASS as for a cached access. The concrete `pl.prefetch` method names and arguments are not established by the registered API extracts. BYPASS can preserve a reread working set by preventing a streaming operand from polluting cache, but a wrong declaration creates a coherency risk. A scope-wide policy saves annotating every implicit read; a per-load policy is more precise and overrides the scope. A prefetch can hide a reload behind existing compute, but a partial or oversized warm adds traffic without a hit. Expecting `BYPASS` to change generated code today; the toolchain warns and emits the cached path. Declaring BYPASS on a tensor that another task writes while the kernel runs. Rebinding the tensor name after a scope declaration and assuming the new value inherits it. Using the benchmark's warm-cache replay as evidence for a cold-cache prefetch strategy.

source_features: joined physical rows == deps.block_num * active kernel_ids slots
items.summary: Chip swimlane timing and dependency topology are separate artifacts joined offline. Level 4 adds scheduler and orchestrator records; `deps.json` proves edges; the critical path and gap attribution explain where makespan went and whether an early-dispatch flag actually staged a task.
items.text: The runtime writes `deps.json` with the task graph: tasks, `kernel_ids`, `block_num`, `early_dispatch`, and annotated edges. It writes `chip_swimlane_records.json` with per-task timing and scheduler/orchestrator phases but no edges. `name_map*.json` maps callable ids to source names, `dispatch_program.json` identifies which program a dispatch directory belongs to, and `swimlane_converter` joins topology and timing into a Perfetto-viewable merge. Joining timing to fanout on the device hot path would cost a GM store and linked-list walk per task, so the join is offline and one `deps.json` can serve many timing runs of the same topology. Capture levels add: level 1 AICore start/end; level 2 AICPU dispatch/finish; level 3 scheduler phase records; level 4 orchestrator phase records. Dispatch attribution, gap attribution, and early-dispatch proof need level 4. A bare `--enable-chip-swimlane` means level 1; request level 4 explicitly. Before trusting a capture, require `chip_swimlane_level == 4`, equal counts for raw AICore rows, raw AICPU rows, and joined rows, and for every timed task `joined physical rows == deps.block_num * active kernel_ids slots`. A dropped SPMD or MIX row can turn a partial early-dispatch result into a false full count. The identity chain is `dispatch_program.json -> next_levels/<program>/kernel_config.py -> name_map*.json::callable_id_to_name -> deps.json::tasks[task_id].kernel_ids -> source name_hint or submitted callee`. A MIX task maps to more than one callable name, and compiler suffixes can be inlined copies of one source hint, so one source site may own several runtime occurrences. The Observed critical path is the as-executed backward blame path through data and same-core predecessors; its task compute plus stalls tile the measured AICore makespan. Static CPM is the duration-weighted longest dependency path assuming unlimited cores. Use Observed to decide where time went and Static CPM as a cross-check; a large gap indicates a scheduling problem, not a graph problem. The makespan covers first AICore start through last AICore end, excluding host/orchestrator front time and the AICPU tail. For a gap before a task, define `data_ready(C) = max(pred.end_time_us)`, `observed_ready(C) = max(pred.finish_time_us)`, `dispatch(C) = min(C block dispatch_time_us)`, and `start(C) = min(C block start_time_us)`. Producer end to producer finish is FIN detection; last producer finish to dispatch is ready-but-undispatched; dispatch to start is pickup/gate. A ready-but-undispatched gap is a scheduler/occupancy claim and requires proving every compatible core lacked a free slot throughout; level-4 scheduler phase records carry counts, not causal task IDs. A pickup gap can be same-core contention only if the occupying task ran until `start(C)`. If dispatch precedes observed readiness, the task was speculatively early-staged and the remaining wait is a gate, not a queue. For early dispatch, structural eligibility requires every direct producer to be an allocation source or carry `early_dispatch=true`, with at least one non-allocation producer; temporal evidence requires `dispatch_time_us + tolerance < max(producer finish_time_us)`, with tolerance about two clock ticks. Report `full N/N`, `partial N/M`, or `none`. If timestamps look early but the graph is not structurally eligible, suspect a stale artifact. A schedule has gaps and the cause could be producer FIN detection, ready-but-undispatched delay, or pickup. A source-level early-dispatch hint needs proof that staging occurred. A distributed capture must be validated before its makespan is trusted. Collect a real-device capture with `--enable-chip-swimlane 4` and add `--enable-dep-gen` for the graph; join streams with `swimlane_converter.read_perf_data()` rather than by hand. Validate counts and the `block_num * active kernel_ids slots` identity before quoting a result. Use `python -m simpler_setup.tools.critical_path <work_dir> --stdout` to reconstruct static and observed paths. Split every critical-path gap into FIN detection, undispatched, and pickup before choosing an early-dispatch, dummy, or occupancy fix. Take production numbers from an unprofiled benchmark; use level 4 for causal evidence only. Runtime task IDs are capture-local execution instances, not source identifiers; they do not survive a rebuild. `deps.json` edge sources are `creator`, `tensormap`, and `explicit`; an edge absent from the graph does not exist at run time. Simulator platforms emit records but skip merged conversion because metadata is incomplete. Level 4 collection has observer cost and perturbs the schedule it measures. A capture with missing SPMD or MIX rows cannot support a full-count claim. Level 4 gives the causal detail needed for dispatch attribution but changes timing; level 1 is lighter but insufficient for gap attribution. Separating topology from timing lets one graph serve many runs but requires an offline join and validation. Observed critical path explains the actual run; static CPM explains the graph's lower structure under unlimited cores. Treating `deps.json::tasks[].early_dispatch` as proof that a task was staged. Using temporal proximity to blame a specific blocking task without proving compatible-core occupancy. Joining raw cycle-domain streams by hand or skipping equal-count validation. Using a `store_true` flag for a capture level that needs an integer; its `True` silently binds to level 1 or the most expensive level depending on the declaration.

source_features: pl.matmul(lhs, rhs, out_dtype=None, a_trans=False, b_trans=False, c_matrix_nz=False)
items.summary: `pl.matmul`, `pl.matmul_acc`, and `pl.matmul_bias` map to the Cube unit; `pl.gemv*` specialize M=1. Float accumulates in FP32 and INT8 in INT32. `init_cond` removes the peeled first K step, but rank and L0C-window rules have unresolved or strict cases.
items.text: `pl.matmul(lhs, rhs, out_dtype=None, a_trans=False, b_trans=False, c_matrix_nz=False)` computes matrix multiplication, with the transpose and C-layout flags applying to the tensor path. At tile level, transposition is a type property, so passing `a_trans` or `b_trans` with a Tile operand raises rather than being ignored. A tensor-level matmul with rank greater than 2 is lowered to batched matmul and then unrolled to per-batch tile matmuls. `pl.matmul_acc(acc, lhs, rhs, init_cond=...)` fuses accumulation. On K steps where `init_cond` holds, `acc` is overwritten with `lhs @ rhs` instead of accumulated into, which is the split-K `k == 0` idiom and removes the need to zero the accumulator or peel the first step. A literal `True`/`False` selects a compile-time form; a runtime predicate lowers to a branch over the two. The accumulator must be allocated inside the InCore region; hoisting it to orchestration makes it GM and ptoas rejects the load. L0C is stored in 16x16 blocks column-major. When `acc` is a window of a larger `Mem.Acc` tile, slice it along columns so the window either spans every row of its parent or is at most 16 columns wide inside a single 16-column block. A row window at `[t0, 0]` out of an `[M, N]` accumulator is strided with more than one block column and is rejected; a column window addresses L0C in the order the hardware writes it. `pl.matmul_bias(lhs, rhs, bias)` fuses a broadcast bias add. `pl.gemv`/`gemv_acc`/`gemv_bias` specialize a one-row left operand; use them when M is 1 because the Cube schedules the smaller form more efficiently. `acc_phase=pl.AccPhase.Partial` and `Final` track producer-side unit-flag chunks; a producer ending in `Final` must be consumed by a store with `st_phase=pl.STPhase.Final`. Batched tile forms are `pl.batch_matmul` and `pl.tile.batch_matmul_acc`; there is no top-level `pl.batch_matmul_acc`. MX forms are `pl.matmul_mx`, `pl.matmul_mx_acc`, and `pl.matmul_mx_bias`, with FP8E4M3FN data and FP8E8M0 scales; an FP4 lhs must be cast to FP8E4M3FN first. Writing a K-loop that accumulates a projection on chip. Choosing GEMV instead of matmul for a one-row decode operand. Splitting K across cores with atomics or an accumulator seed. Using MX block-scaled matmul or quantizing for it. Use `acc = pl.matmul_acc(acc, tile_a, tile_b, init_cond=(kb == 0))` inside the K loop and allocate `acc` inside the `pl.at` or `pl.spmd` body. Slice an accumulator along columns, for example `acc_n = pl.slice(acc, [M, N_TILE], [0, n0 * N_TILE])`, rather than taking a row band of a multi-block-column parent. Use `pl.gemv` or `pl.gemv_acc` for M=1 and `pl.matmul` for larger M. Use `out_dtype` only for conversions the FIXPIPE can perform; use explicit `pl.cast` for INT32->FP32, FP32->INT8, or INT32->INT8. For MX quantization, use `pl.quant_mx` with `group_axis` matching the operand, then stage data and scales through GM before `matmul_mx`. `init_cond` is documented for 2D operands in the installed API, but the operations guide demonstrates a rank-3 grouped GEMM predicate. Rank-greater-than-2 `init_cond` is unresolved; avoid it unless the exact compiler accepts it. When the left operand narrows to a runtime row count and the accumulator is taller than one 16-row fractal, `mad` writes compact rows while a non-compact accumulator is read at its physical row count; `init_cond` alone then fails `AccCompactValid`. A compile-time-constant valid shape or an accumulator of at most 16 rows is unaffected. `a_trans`, `b_trans`, and `c_matrix_nz` are Tensor-only and raise with Tile operands. The Tile-level `pl.tile.matmul` has no `out_dtype`; the unified entry accepts `out_dtype` on tiles only when it agrees with the cube deduction. On tensors, `out_dtype` is limited to FIXPIPE conversions: FP32/FP16/BF16 for float operands and INT32 for int operands. `matmul_bias` bias has shape `[1, N]` and the accumulator dtype. MX data tiles reaching `matmul_mx` must both be FP8E4M3FN; native FP4xFP4 and reverse FP8xFP4 are unsupported. `pl.quant_mx` is MXFP8-only in this release; `group_axis=1` is the A-side `[M, K]` path with `M%16==0` and `K%64==0`, while `group_axis=0` is the B-side `[N, K]` path with `N%32==0` and `K%64==0`. It cannot currently share one InCore mixed task with `matmul_mx`; stage quantized data and scale through GM between AIV and AIC. `matmul_acc` keeps the partial sum on chip and removes a zeroing step, but ties the accumulator to one L0C buffer and strict window geometry. GEMV schedules a smaller Cube form for M=1, but requires the one-row and dtype conditions. A fused bias saves an epilogue dispatch but restricts the bias shape. MX reduces operand width and memory, but adds scale layout, dtype, and cross-core transport restrictions. Hoisting the accumulator out of the InCore region; ptoas rejects the accumulator load. Slicing an L0C accumulator by rows rather than columns. Requesting `out_dtype=pl.FP32` on INT8 operands; that is a dequantization and raises. Using `init_cond` with a runtime-narrowed row count and a tall accumulator without the required seed/peel form. Trying to place `quant_mx` and `matmul_mx` in one mixed InCore task without staging through GM.

source_features: Acc bytes ~= M_tile * N_tile * accumulator_bytes * live_accumulators
Mat bytes ~= (M_tile + N_tile * live_weights) * K_tile * input_bytes * buffering_factor
items.summary: Choose M, N, and K by ranking shapes, rejecting them against the compiler's Mat/Acc/Vec report, then measuring survivors. Growing N or K increases the L1 weight fragment; growing M or N increases the L0C accumulator; a K-contiguous transfer below the cache-line floor can lose more than a wider N gains.
items.text: Record the full M x N x K, operand and accumulator element sizes, the row tile, N fragment, K fragment, number of live weights and accumulators, whether the weight is K-contiguous (`[N, K]`, often with `b_trans=True`) or N-contiguous (`[K, N]`), pipeline depth, and production row occupancy. Use separate tile constants for unrelated matmuls; one shared constant lets the most constrained task cap every other task and makes a sweep hard to interpret. Cube fragments are constrained mainly by Mat and Acc; vector fragments by Vec and transfer pattern. If one shared fragment forces both tasks to the smaller value, give each its own tile constants. When program structure permits, split the scopes through a GM intermediate so each phase can choose its own fragment, but count the added traffic and confirm the end-to-end result. Under the default planner, the compiler memory report at `build_output/<case>/report/memory_after_AllocateMemoryAddr.txt` is ground truth. `Mat` is L1 operand storage and a hard user-visible constraint. `Acc` is L0C and is often a soft boundary because a plain matmul output can be compiler-subtiled, but each extra output tile adds a FIXPIPE drain and may restream operands. `Vec` is the UB/vector constraint. `Left` and `Right` are compiler-derived L0 staging; do not shrink a DSL tile merely to reduce their percentages. Useful estimates are `Acc bytes ~= M_tile * N_tile * accumulator_bytes * live_accumulators` and `Mat bytes ~= (M_tile + N_tile * live_weights) * K_tile * input_bytes * buffering_factor`; a contiguous weight fragment is `K_tile * input_bytes`. The real allocation includes alignment, padding, liveness, and backend transforms. On A2/A3, an innermost transfer below 512 bytes can move a full cache line while using only part of it; for a K-contiguous weight, keep `K_tile * input_bytes >= 512` when feasible. For grouped or MoE GEMMs, the row tile controls how often a weight is restreamed: cover a typical group in one row tile if Mat and Acc allow. Sweep in rounds: isolate row, N, K, or grouping; combine the best two or three; push the remaining axis until the report or compile failure identifies the wall; stop when a complete round does not improve beyond noise. Use identical seeded inputs and compare one benchmark's mean field with the same warmup and rounds. A cube scope is important to end-to-end time and its M/N/K tile is still a free variable. A grouped or MoE GEMM repeatedly restreams the same weight because a typical group spans more rows than one row tile. Cube and vector consumers want different output fragments but share one constant. The build report shows that one shared fragment is forcing both cube and vector phases to a smaller value. Give each matmul its own `M_TILE`, `N_TILE`, and `K_TILE` constants; do not share one global tile across unrelated tasks. When N or K hits Mat, reduce K to buy room, reduce simultaneously live weights, or reduce N; when M or N hits Acc, check for compiler sub-tiling and its FIXPIPE cost. Widen the innermost K transfer until `K_tile * input_bytes >= 512` on A2/A3, then re-check the Mat footprint. When cube and vector fragments conflict, use distinct constants; split the phases through a GM intermediate only when independent tuning is worth the extra traffic. Mat 512 KiB, Acc 128 KiB, Vec compiler-safe 184 KiB within 192 KiB UB, and Left/Right 64 KiB each are local 910B4 capacities, not performance results. L0C sub-tiling is not guaranteed for `matmul_acc`, vector or PV left operands, or mixed on-chip consumers; compile the exact candidate program. A K-contiguous transfer below the target's cache-line size may still be correct but inefficient. Changing the M/N/K fragment changes Mat, Acc, and sometimes Vec; Left/Right are derived underneath it. A GM split for independent cube and vector fragments may add traffic or be performance-neutral; confirm end to end. Under the default PYPTO planner, read the build memory report. Under PTOAS, address allocation is skipped, so do not rely on address-dependent artifacts and judge the exact compile or run. Larger tiles improve utilization and reduce small MTE transactions but consume L1/L0C and can force sub-tiling or fail to compile. Covering a whole MoE group in one row tile avoids weight restreaming but raises the row footprint. Decoupling cube and vector fragments exposes independent tuning axes but may be neutral or add GM traffic. A shared fragment is simpler and may be sufficient when one consumer is not on the critical path. Tuning against an unrealistically small test input that does not represent production row occupancy. Using one shared tile constant and concluding the most constrained task's limit applies to all matmuls. Shrinking a tile to lower `Left`/`Right` percentages rather than reading `Mat`, `Acc`, and `Vec`. Treating a formula as proof of optimality; the actual build report and repeated device measurement are authoritative. Assuming decoupling cube and vector fragments always improves end-to-end time; the split can cost more than the smaller fragment did.

Producer lookup for `In` and `InOut` arguments adds an edge to the current registered producer of any overlapping region. Producer registration for `Out` and `InOut` makes this task the producer of that buffer. Thus RAW and WAW are tracked. The scheduler evaluates the comparison at the dispatch point, after this task's dependencies are satisfied, so the value is current. If false, the task is retired inline and never reaches a core, while its fanin and fanout still settle so downstream consumers unlock normally. items.summary: Gather and scatter have index and mask forms with different rank, index-width, and destination-stride rules. Sort/top-k is single-row: `sort32` produces interleaved value-index runs and `mrgsort` merges them using a block length measured in interleaved positions.
items.text: `pl.gather` is a unified tensor-level operation with index, mask, and compare forms. The index form computes `output[b, k] = input[b, index[b, k]]`, is rank-2 with `dim=-1` in the MVP, and requires the index as a real tensor rather than a computed tile. The mask form selects fixed lane patterns, with `P0101` taking even lanes and `P1010` taking odd lanes; this is the RoPE de-interleave operation. `pl.scatter` is the inverse family. Its tensor index form writes `output[b, index[b, k]] = src[b, k]` and requires the index element width to match the input width; its mask form writes compact source rows into mask-selected columns of a destination with the required stride. At tile level, `scatter` uses flattened destination offsets with the same shape as the source, while `scatter_mask` is the mask inverse of `gather_mask`. Sorting is a separate primitive set. `pl.sort32` sorts each contiguous 32-element block in descending order while carrying an index ramp; the output is an interleaved value-index array. `pl.mrgsort` then 4-way-merges adjacent sorted blocks. Its `block_len` is the input run length in interleaved positions, not the element count, and it must be a multiple of 64. `sort32` leaves 64-position runs, so each stage grows the run by four. Top-k is built by sorting the row, slicing the leading `2*k` interleaved pairs, and gathering the odd lanes for the index list. Both sort primitives require a single row; multi-row tiles must loop over rows. `pl.arange` supplies the index ramp but populates only the first row, so use `[1, N]` shapes. For tensor scatter, keep `src` and `index` the same shape and match the index element width to the input width; for mask scatter, size `dst` by the pattern stride. For top-k, start with `pl.arange(0, [1, N], dtype=pl.UINT32)`, use `pl.sort32`, then the required `pl.mrgsort` chain, slice the leading `2*k` pairs, and gather odd lanes. Loop rows explicitly for multi-row sort; do not pass a multi-row tile to `sort32` or `mrgsort`. `pl.gather` index form is rank-2 and `dim=-1` only in the MVP; the index is INT32, or INT16 with a 16-bit input, and has the same rank as the input. At tile level the index must be a real tensor from `pl.create_tensor`, not a `pl.full` tile; the tensor path allocates needed scratch during conversion. `pl.gather` mask form uses `P0101` for even lanes and `P1010` for odd lanes, shrinking the last dimension by 2; other patterns shrink by 4 or preserve it for `P1111`. `output_dtype` is a same-width bit reinterpretation, not a numeric cast. `pl.scatter` tensor index form is the column-wise inverse of gather: `src` and `index` are `[rows, K]`, the input is `[rows, S]` with `K <= S`, and the index element width must match the input width. For a multi-row tile, loop the rows with `pl.range`. `pl.arange`/`pl.ci` populate only the first row and prefer `[1, N]` shapes. items.text: On 220x, each AI Core contains an AIC for Cube computation and an AIV for Vector computation, each with its own Scalar Unit and code segment. Data between AIV and AIC moves through global memory. Vector data from UB must be 32-byte aligned. The Cube accesses L0A for the left operand, L0B for the right, and L0C for products and intermediate results. Recommended fractal layouts are L0A `FRACTAL_ZZ`, L0B `FRACTAL_ZN`, L0C `FRACTAL_NZ`, and L1 `FRACTAL_NZ`; the Unified Buffer has no required data format. UB and L1 accesses use 32-byte granularity, L0A/L0B transfers use 512-byte granularity, and L0C/Bias accesses use 64-byte granularity. FixPipe is operand-specific in the local CANN 9.0.0 source: `ReluPreAddr` is encoded in FPC[7:0] after shifting by 6 (64-byte address units), while `QuantPreAddr` is encoded in FPC[15:8] after shifting by 7 (128-byte address units). The Quant_PRE helper rounds dequant data up to 128 bytes and uses 128-byte CBUF-to-FBUF bursts. The separate 64-byte/128-byte values in the architecture and constraints material therefore describe different fields or transfer contexts rather than a single contradiction. A generic temporary-FBUF offset check in CPU debug accepts 32-byte alignment, but that API check does not relax the 128-byte unit required when the address is encoded as QuantPre. DMA to UB is aligned to the data block size; DMA to other units is aligned to fractal requirements. Moving NZ data from L1 to L0A requires ZZ conversion, and if the remaining L1 size is less than one fractal, hardware execution can fault. UB bank conflicts occur when multiple operations access the same bank or bank group at once; staggering addresses can reduce read/write and write/write queues. GM accesses to the same address by multiple cores are serialized by hardware, so multi-core access should be staggered and a tiling policy should let the first load populate L2. Moving more than 16 KiB at a time generally improves bandwidth utilization, but the best size is chip-dependent. GM-to-L1 `DataCopy` has a source-block gap limit of 65535 data blocks of 32 bytes; a larger gap requires splitting the instruction. Data movement is split into 128-, 256-, or 512-byte chunks and non-aligned lengths are rounded up, so aligning the inner axis pays. Scalar writes to GM are cached in DCache and hardware does not ensure DCache/GM consistency; use `DataCacheCleanAndInvalid` or the PyPTO cache-publication sequence. Cross-core flag counters have a limit and must be used in matched pairs; PyPTO/PTO extern code is not automatically synchronized by the Ascend C framework's LocalTensor rules. items.summary: `pl.range`, `pl.unroll`, `pl.parallel`, `pl.pipeline`, and `pl.spmd` share syntax but carry different compiler promises. The IR is SSA, so values crossing a loop or branch are carried explicitly or through parser-inserted `pl.yield_`.
items.text: `pl.range` is a strict sequential loop and is legal both outside and inside `pl.at`. `pl.unroll` is sequential with compile-time replication; its bounds must be literal and it rejects `init_values`. `pl.parallel` asserts that iterations are independent and may be distributed across cores; it belongs in orchestration, not inside `pl.at`. `pl.pipeline` is a sequential InCore loop that software-pipelines stages; it requires `stage=N` and belongs inside `pl.at`. `pl.spmd` is a parallel SPMD loop whose body is implicitly InCore; it belongs outside `pl.at` and takes only a block count, with start fixed at 0 and step 1. Rebinding a name inside a loop is the ordinary way to carry a value: the parser renames it and threads it through as an `IterArg`, even though the IR has no mutation. `init_values=` plus `pl.yield_` is the explicit spelling, and it is mandatory for `pl.while_`. A loop result is read from the name bound by `yield_`, not from the initializer name. `pl.while_` also requires `pl.cond(...)` as the first statement of its body. A branch that produces a value must yield from both arms with the same arity and types. `strict_ssa=True` rejects rebinding and disables subscript-write sugar. Choosing sequential versus parallel versus pipelined iteration. Accumulating a result across iterations without relying on mutation semantics. Avoiding a race caused by declaring independent iterations that actually share state. Use `pl.parallel` for independent batch or tile chunks; reserve `pl.range` for carried state, ordered accumulation, or an InCore loop that should not be distributed. Use `for i in pl.pipeline(0, K // K_STEP, stage=2):` for a matmul K loop so the next tile's load can overlap current compute. Use `for i, (acc,) in pl.range(N, init_values=(zero,)): acc = pl.yield_(pl.add(acc, x[i]))` when state must be explicit; otherwise rebind `acc = pl.add(acc, x[i])`. Use `for (x,) in pl.while_(init_values=(0,)):` with `pl.cond(x < 10)` as the first body statement. `pl.parallel` is an assertion, not a request to remove dependencies; if iterations are not independent, the result is a race. `pl.unroll` has no carried values and accepts only compile-time constant bounds. `pl.pipeline` requires a positive `stage` and cannot appear outside `pl.at`; `pl.spmd` cannot appear inside `pl.at` and does not take start/stop/step. Every carried value must keep one level and type through the loop. Mixing a tensor-level value with a tile-level value inside an InCore scope does not type-check. `pl.yield_` binds all carried values simultaneously; code generation orders the copies by byte overlap, but an author-level swap needs scratch. `pl.parallel` exposes cross-core parallelism but requires genuine independence and can increase scheduling pressure. `pl.unroll` removes loop overhead and index math but increases code size and instruction-cache pressure. `pl.pipeline` buys load/compute overlap but needs `stage` copies of live buffers and can overflow on-chip memory. A loop inside one InCore kernel removes dispatches but serializes work that could otherwise run on other cores. items.summary: `AllocateMemoryAddr` gives concrete addresses to non-DDR MemRefs. PYPTO uses deterministic 32-byte-aligned sequential allocation per space; DSA_RP solves capacity-constrained placement with reuse penalties; PTOAS skips the pass. `pl.reserve_buffer` and cross-core pipe rings can dominate an overflow.
items.text: Under `MemoryPlanner.PYPTO`, `AllocateMemoryAddr` collects unique MemRefs and assigns each memory space its own address range starting from zero unless a reserve buffer already reserved a leading window. Addresses are 32-byte aligned, MemRefs are sorted by name for determinism, and DDR is skipped. View MemRefs that share a base pointer are co-located in one slot sized by the largest member; each view keeps its relative byte offset, so a reshape of a slice that does not emit a subview still reads the correct offset. Under `MemoryPlanner.DSA_RP`, the pass builds an in-memory problem with hard lifetime interference, reserved ranges, semantic no-alias, target hazards, requested pipeline-stage separation, and hard arena capacity. Author-declared MemRefs are hard-separated. Soft unit-weight pairs model recognized cross-pipe WAR/WAW handoffs to discourage costly physical reuse. Canonical greedy tries offset zero, reserved-range ends, and aligned tops of placed neighbors, chooses the lowest incremental penalty and then the lowest address, and validates every placement. Pipeline intent is strict-then-soft: solve with all requested separations hard; if no fitting placement is found, relax only pipeline-intent pairs, add unit penalties, and solve again; if the relaxed placement overlaps a pair, emit `PH-DSA-001`. A no-fit result is a bounded-search failure, not an infeasibility certificate. DSA_RP depends on ptoas InsertSync recognizing physical range overlap across allocation roots; older ptoas releases are incompatible. `MemoryPlanner.PTOAS` skips address allocation and leaves placement to ptoas. `system.reserve_buffer(base=AUTO)` reserves a named leading window and is resolved to an explicit base; its bytes are counted in the high-water mark but are not a MemRef and are invisible in per-tile accounting. The cross-core pipe ring is `slot_size * slot_num` bytes in the consuming core's memory: Mat/L1 for V2C (`pl.aic_gather`), Vec/UB for C2V (`pl.aiv_shard`). `slot_size` is the full tile the consumer pops, and `slot_num` defaults to 2. Lower the depth with `optimizations=[pl.cross_core_slot(slot_num=N)]` on the enclosing `pl.at(...)` or shrink the crossing tile. items.summary: `MemoryReuse` coalesces tiles with non-overlapping lifetimes in the same space, subject to no-alias constraints and a pipeline-stage capacity guard. Author-declared `pl.MemRef` allocations are pinned and isolated; they trade capacity for scheduling independence and have planner-specific restrictions.
items.text: `MemoryReuse` computes lifetimes by def-use analysis, including nested control flow and loop-aware extension. Two tiles are non-overlapping when the previous tile's last use is at or before the next tile's definition; inputs are read before outputs are written in one statement. Same-space, lifetime-disjoint intervals can share a MemRef. The packer is global largest-first, and a buffer's size is fixed by its largest member, so a later smaller interval can join an earlier larger buffer and a later larger interval can host an earlier smaller one. Shape, dtype, and `TileView` need not match: each variable keeps its own static descriptor on the shared base. The pass removes alloc statements whose MemRef is no longer referenced. A no-alias guard forbids a reused output from sharing the physical buffer of an operand that is read while the output is written. It covers `tile.recip`, `tile.rsqrt`, row reductions, `tile.mrgsort_format1`, `tile.move`, remainder ops, `tile.transpose`, `tile.sel` and `tile.sels`, `tile.prelu`, row/column expands, and widening `tile.cast`. The guard resolves operands through both reuse-map coalescing and view inheritance, so a forbidden operand reached indirectly is still caught. A pipeline guard keeps concurrent cloned stages in distinct buffers up to an affordable depth; collapsing concurrent clones onto one buffer injects a false WAR and serializes stages. The capacity gate uses an exact per-space footprint and emits `PH-MR-001` when it reduces depth. The pipeline guard applies to the replication path; under PTOAS an eligible loop is claimed earlier by slot rotation and `MemoryReuse` is skipped for that pipeline. A declared allocation is written as `scratch = pl.MemRef()` and referenced by variable in a tile annotation. InitMemRef makes it `tile.alloc(..., pinned=True)`, and `MemoryReuse` treats it as closed: a pinned interval opens its own slot and that slot is skipped for every later candidate program. Tiles bound to different declared buffers are never coalesced; tiles bound to the same buffer already share a base. On a `slots=N` declaration, co-liveness is checked per slot: two tiles on different slots are meant to be live together, only two tiles on the same slot corrupt each other. A runtime slot index has no static slot to attribute, so that check is skipped; the rotation is the author's responsibility. Declared allocations are rejected under PTOAS and hard-separated in DSA_RP, subject to the multi-slot caveat above. On Ascend910B AIV functions with a non-`None` split mode, a writer that consumes both a load result and a `tile.tpop_from_aic` value must not place its output in the same physical buffer as the load result; the pass guards that hardware hazard. Let lifetime-disjoint tiles reuse memory by default; inspect a memory map before forcing more reuse. Declare `scratch = pl.MemRef()` and annotate tiles with it when an allocation must remain independent of the packer. Use `l0c = pl.MemRef(slots=2)` and `l0c[i % 2]` for an explicit ping-pong, keeping one slot live per iteration for PTOAS portability. Do not pin every buffer: pinning trades capacity for scheduling independence and surfaces as a hard allocation overflow rather than being coalesced back. Reuse requires non-overlapping lifetime and the same memory space; different shapes, dtypes, or views are permitted. A declared allocation's co-live tiles must agree on memory space. items.text: `pl.at(level=pl.Level.CORE_GROUP)` lowers to an InCore kernel, and a mixed region can contain Cube and Vector work. `pl.cluster()` groups AIC and AIV kernels so they are co-scheduled on one physical cluster, producing a `Group` function. `for aiv_id in pl.split_aiv(2, mode=...)` opens a structural AIV-split region. `mode=pl.SplitMode.UP_DOWN` or `LEFT_RIGHT` halves every tile along rows or columns, so each lane works on half. `mode=pl.SplitMode.NONE` keeps the full body on both lanes; the author dispatches disjoint work with `aiv_id`. Opening even one region changes the contract for the whole function: vector compute must live inside a region, Cube ops and barriers stay outside, and every tile crossing a region edge must be named. A cube-produced value read on the vector lane uses `pl.aiv_shard`; a vector-produced value read on the cube lane uses `pl.aic_gather`. An unnamed crossing is rejected even though codegen could emit the same transfer; the point is that the boundary was chosen. In `mode=NONE` both ops preserve shape; in a data-parallel mode they halve or rejoin along the split axis. `pl.aiv_shard` of a value already produced on the vector lane is rejected because there is no AIC-to-AIV crossing. All `aiv_shard`/`aic_gather` calls in one function ride one logical cross-core pipe, and the pipe is fixed as split or no-split for its lifetime. A `NONE` region that crosses cannot sit beside an `UP_DOWN`/`LEFT_RIGHT` region that crosses; two different split axes are fine because only split-versus-no-split belongs to the pipe. A value gathered out of a `NONE` region must be lane-uniform: both AIV lanes push to one slot with no per-lane offset, and if they hold different values the Cube receives an unspecified one. This is not diagnosed. GM traffic is outside the tile-crossing rules: if one lane writes a GM buffer and another reads it, publish producer cache lines and fence, place a cross-core barrier, then invalidate the consumer cache before reading. `pl.system.syncall` synchronizes arrival only. A conservative sequence is `pl.system.cacheinvalid(); pl.system.fence(); pl.system.syncall(mode=pl.SyncAllMode.SOFT, core_type=pl.KernelType.MIX, gm_workspace=sync_ws, used_cores=participant_count); pl.system.cacheinvalid()`, where `sync_ws` is an exclusive zero-initialized 16-element INT32 GM tensor. A cross-rank notify or a GM handoff between AIC and AIV must be ordered correctly. Place a Cube matmul and its vector epilogue in one `pl.at(level=pl.Level.CORE_GROUP)` with a split optimization when buffers fit; use `pl.cluster()` when the group must be a separate Group function. Write one `for ... in pl.split_aiv(2, mode=...)` region per vector phase, with `pl.aiv_shard` at entry for C2V values and `pl.aic_gather` before returning a V2C value. Shard a once-only notify as `for owner in pl.range(aiv_id, NUM_PEERS, 2):`, or guard it with `if aiv_id == 0:` only when lane 0 wrote the released data. Use the full cache-publication, `fence`, `syncall`, cache-invalidation sequence for a multi-line GM handoff; use `syncall(mode=pl.SyncAllMode.SOFT, core_type=pl.KernelType.MIX, gm_workspace=sync_ws, used_cores=...)` when a barrier is required. `pl.split_aiv` accepts only `n=2`; `mode` is required. A region that contains cube compute is rejected; Cube work stays outside every region. Authoring `split_aiv` directly in an `InCore` function is rejected; write it in a plain `@pl.jit` or Opaque body. The region is a structural node and is nestable in loops or conditionals, but all crossings in one function must agree on split-versus-no-split; use separate `pl.at` scopes to give phases separate pipes. Only a lane-uniform value may be gathered out of a `mode=NONE` region; the compiler does not diagnose a violation. If the lanes must contribute different data, route through GM and order it or use a data-parallel region. The compiler keeps region comm ops off the Cube lane, but it does not check whether both AIV lanes ran the same notify. A lane-0 guard is safe only when lane 0 wrote all data the signal releases; otherwise shard the notify or order both lanes. `syncall` aligns arrival, not data visibility; cache publication and invalidation are separate. The tensor-region cacheinvalid overload covers only the cache line containing the view base; use the whole-GM form for multi-line buffers. `ExpandMixedKernel` automatically handles only one narrow C->V case: a unique cube `tile.store` producer whose same-origin vector `tile.load` is in the same or a nested body. Every other GM handoff remains manual. A mixed kernel removes a hand-off and lets Cube and Vector overlap, but manual split mode restricts where vector and cube work may live. Data-parallel split halves per-lane work but requires halving/rejoining crossings; `NONE` preserves shapes but forbids differing lane values at a gather. A soft GM-polling barrier works at partial occupancy; a hard FFTS barrier requires full-core occupancy. Sharding a notify preserves correctness at the cost of more control logic per lane. items.summary: A golden must compute the same operation order and dtype as the kernel. When it does not, use `error_distribution` to see the error shape, `golden_data` to pin inputs, and `pl.dump_tag` with partial dump to find the first divergent stage. items.text: The golden is the device-emulating reference, so it must mirror the kernel's operation order and its dtype at every step. Floating-point arithmetic is non-associative and lossy at each narrowing; an algebraically equivalent reorder, a folded scale, a different accumulation order, or a cast at a different point changes the last bits. When the golden deliberately reorders an algebraically equivalent op for the kernel's benefit, align the golden to the kernel's order; when the golden is ground truth, such as an RNE cast, fix the kernel. The `error_distribution` comparator is a measurement, never a failing gate. It prints whole-tensor rel-L2 and cosine, a `frac>thd` table, and percentiles of relative diff, absolute diff, and golden magnitude. The magnitude row distinguishes a large relative diff on a near-zero output from a real error. Custom levels use `error_distribution(diff_thds=(...), quantiles=(...))`. After seeing the shape, choose a real gate such as `ratio_allclose` or `ratio_reldiff` at the threshold and bad-point budget the distribution justifies. To localize a stage, pin inputs with `golden_data=<dir>`, tag suspects with `pl.dump_tag(t)`, run with `enable_dump_args=1`, and compare each dumped intermediate against its torch reference in dependency order. The first stage whose distribution blows up is the culprit; downstream stages inherit its error. `pl.dump_tag` is forward-sticky over the enclosing orchestration: it affects every subsequent kernel dispatch consuming that exact tensor value, tracked by Var identity. Rebinding the name after a tag produces a new value that the old tag does not cover. The marker only fires when the tagged Var reaches a dispatch as a static whole-tensor argument. It is silently not dumped for a dynamic-offset read that lowers to a gather, an orchestration-level `pl.assemble` that emits only a name alias, an orchestration-tier scalar read, or a host-tier distributed SubWorker tensor. `dumps=[...]` on `pl.submit` or `pl.at` is the explicit per-launch counterpart. Full dump captures every binding and can saturate the host collector; partial dump filters to tagged tensors. `golden_data` replay removes torch recomputation when only timing changes. Use seeded test input and real weights: random data can hide a dynamic-range quantization error, and per-element relative diff is meaningless near zero. Report rel-L2 or cosine for real-weight runs. Pin inputs with `golden_data=<dir>` and tag only a few suspect intermediates with `pl.dump_tag(t)` under `enable_dump_args=1`. Walk dumped intermediates in dependency order and stop at the first distribution that blows up. For real-weight validation, extract the converted checkpoint per layer, cast each tensor to its spec dtype, and override via `TensorSpec.init_value`; seed the test input. `error_distribution` always passes; it is not a correctness gate. The marker does not cover dynamic-offset reads, orchestration `pl.assemble` aliases, orchestration scalar reads, or L3 HOST-tier SubWorker tensors. Torch's `.to(dtype)` uses round-to-nearest ties-to-even, so a narrowing cast intended to match torch must pass `mode='rint'`; the default differs on exact ties. Use `rint` for fp32-to-bf16, fp32-to-fp16, fp32-to-int8 quantizers, and integer dequantization that needs rounded conversion. Use `none` for an Acc-to-Vec or other width-preserving move. Use `trunc` or `floor` for float-to-int index or lane math, never ties-away, which can jump an index. Keep activations and intermediates at the highest precision that is free, usually fp32, and narrow only where a bf16, fp16, or int8 consumer requires it. Never cast through an intermediate narrowing: fp32-to-uint8 or fp32-to-int8 should quantize directly from fp32, not via bf16 or fp16, because the intermediate hop discards mantissa bits before quantization. The same applies to dequantization: go from the integer to fp32, not through fp16. PyPTO has no implicit promotion; every width change needs an explicit cast. A narrow op may lower to one hardware `pto.tcvt` or a chain of conversions depending on target; a multi-hop chain can differ from a directly rounded conversion by one destination ULP. preconditions: Choosing whether a computation belongs at tensor, tile, or block level.

risks: Assuming source order orders two dispatches: the runtime may overlap them, producing an intermittent race.

items.summary: PyPTO separates what to compute, where it runs, and when it runs: Python builds IR, function type and level select the control or execution plane, and the runtime schedules a derived task graph. Source adjacency is not an ordering guarantee.
items.text: A PyPTO program is authored in Python, but Python is not the execution engine. Decorators parse source into an immutable SSA IR; passes lower it; code generation emits device kernels plus host orchestration; the runtime builds tasks and schedules whatever is ready. Tensor level names whole DDR arrays and lets the compiler choose placement and data movement. Tile level names on-chip buffers and explicit `pl.load`, `pl.move`, and `pl.store`. Block level names core groups with `pl.at`, `pl.spmd`, or `pl.cluster`. Orchestration is the control plane: it allocates tensors and dispatches work, but never touches tile memory. InCore is the execution plane: it loads, computes, and stores, but does not allocate orchestration tensors or dispatch work. `Opaque` has no committed plane until used, and `Inline` leaves no function because it is spliced into callers. `pl.at(level=pl.Level.CORE_GROUP)` outlines a region into an InCore kernel; `@pl.jit.incore` names such a kernel directly. The hardware cluster is one Cube core and two Vector cores, which is why mixed kernels and cross-core pipelines exist. Because the runtime derives dependencies from buffers and declared edges, two dispatches are ordered only when something establishes an edge; writing one after another in source establishes nothing. Reasoning about why two dispatches overlap even though they are written sequentially. Use `@pl.jit` for an orchestration entry and `@pl.jit.incore` for a device kernel; use `with pl.at(level=pl.Level.CORE_GROUP):` for an inline device region. Use tensor-level operators when the compiler should choose placement; use `pl.load`/`pl.move`/`pl.store` when the tile buffer and movement are the point. Name a reusable core group with `pl.cluster()` and a multi-block launch with `pl.spmd(n)` rather than relying on statement order or repeated small scopes. An orchestration body cannot contain device operators directly; place them in an InCore function or `pl.at(level=pl.Level.CORE_GROUP)` scope. `pl.create_tensor` is control-plane allocation; inside a `pl.at` or `pl.spmd` body the allocation becomes a tile, not a GM tensor. The compiler parses source; it does not execute Python control flow. Runtime values that drive ordering must be represented as buffers, scalars, predicates, or TaskIds. A mixed Cube+Vector region remains one task, not several, and an SPMD launch remains one task with multiple logical blocks. Tensor level is shorter and easier to change; tile level buys control over residency, tiling, and movement but exposes buffer lifetime and layout constraints. Splitting into named `.incore` functions improves reuse and code clarity; inline `pl.at` reduces boilerplate but can hide a large kernel body. Explicit placement can avoid compiler conservatism, but every placement choice becomes an invariant the author must maintain. Assuming source order orders two dispatches: the runtime may overlap them, producing an intermittent race. Using whole-tensor operations in a `@pl.jit` body: they are misplaced control-plane/execution-plane operations and are rejected. Allocating a tensor inside a device kernel instead of taking it as an output parameter or allocating it in orchestration. Calling a tile-level `pl.matmul` with operands that are not in `Left` or `Right`; the matmul path requires explicit staging.

items.summary: Row and column reductions collapse different axes and have different scratch-tile contracts on tensor versus tile APIs. Broadcast expansions are single hardware ops, comparison masks need `sel` scratch, and precision flags are operation-specific.
items.text: Reductions are direction-specific. `row_max`, `row_min`, `row_sum`, and `row_prod` reduce the last axis and keep the dimension, so an `[M, N]` input gives `[M, 1]`. `col_max`, `col_min`, `col_sum`, and `col_prod` reduce axis `-2`, so the same input gives `[1, N]`. The tensor and tile APIs share names but differ in scratch ownership. A tensor reduction allocates its own scratch during tensor-to-tile lowering, so the user must omit `tmp_tile`. A tile reduction sees only tile values and therefore requires caller scratch where the hardware needs it: row reductions require the same dtype and rank with dimensions at least as large as the input, while arg reductions require exactly the same shape and dtype. `col_sum` is special: passing `tmp_tile` selects a binary-tree reduction with logarithmic depth and different rounding; omitting it keeps the sequential path. Broadcast operations such as `row_expand_mul`, `row_expand_add`, `col_expand_mul`, and `col_expand_div` are single hardware operations and should be preferred to manually reshaping a vector and relying on elementwise broadcast. Comparison operations return a packed predicate mask; materializing selected values requires `sel` or `sels` with its scratch tile. Precision controls are operation-specific. `rsqrt` takes `high_precision` on the Tensor API and a `tmp` tile on the Tile API; `div` has a high-precision form only for tensor/tensor or tile/tile; `log` and `recip` expose their own high-precision flags. On this hardware a half-data vector reduction can be slower than fp32 because the half writeback is not 32-byte aligned, so use fp32 when the reduction itself is the bottleneck and cast the result only where needed. For a `col_sum` that needs binary-tree depth or precision, pass the matching scratch tile; otherwise omit it for the sequential path. Explicit tile scratch enables on-chip reduction but consumes UB and must match strict shape rules. `col_sum` binary-tree reduction can improve depth and precision but costs scratch and changes rounding. fp32 reduction can be faster and more accurate than half but doubles bytes. items.summary: A runtime scope is both a dependency-tracking boundary and a heap tier. Four ring sets are selected by scope nesting depth, so placing scopes changes when intermediate GM tensors are reclaimed. Memory is freed at scope exit and FIFO reclaim, not at last use.
items.text: The runtime provides an implicit top-level scope, so writing scopes is control and tuning, never a correctness requirement by itself. AUTO mode keeps the producer-map dependency tracking on; MANUAL mode turns it off and makes every edge author-owned. By default the compiler inserts AUTO scopes around a function body and around each `for` and `if` body. A runtime scope also selects one of four ring sets by scope nesting depth: depth 0 uses ring 0, depth 1 ring 1, depth 2 ring 2, and depth 3 or deeper is clamped to ring 3. Each ring has its own task-window slots, output heap, and dependency-edge pool, reclaimed FIFO by its own watermark. A flat kernel can therefore put everything on ring 0 and leave the other rings idle. A `pl.create_tensor` in orchestration becomes a kernel-less allocation task on the current ring. Its block is released only when every consumer has completed and the owning scope has closed; the scope holds its own fanout reference until scope exit. Consequently memory is not freed at last use, a loop without an inner scope accumulates every iteration's intermediates, and one long-lived allocation at the head of a ring can block all later allocations behind it. Deep nesting past depth 3 concentrates pressure on ring 3. Very fine scopes are also scheduling boundaries and cost bookkeeping. The practical fix is usually scope placement: put one scope around a layer and an inner scope around a token block, keep loop-carried values and output parameters outside the inner ownership, and allocate GM scratch outside the `pl.at` that first writes it. Ring sizing is a second fix: `RunConfig` fields `ring_task_window`, `ring_heap`, and `ring_dep_pool` take a scalar broadcast to all four rings or four per-ring values, with 0 meaning the compile default. The process-wide `PTO2_RING_*` environment variables are retired. The source's a2a3 documented defaults are 16384 task slots, 256 MiB heap, and 16384 dependency entries per ring, with a global 65536-entry tensormap; treat those as defaults to verify, not local measurements. A loop allocates intermediates every iteration and never reclaims them before the enclosing scope ends. A runtime allocation must be initialized without the removed `init_value` prefilling surface. Set `@pl.jit(auto_scope=False)` or `@pl.jit.inline(auto_scope=False)` and write `with pl.scope():` around the layer or token block that should own intermediate lifetime. Create loop-carried ping-pong buffers and outputs outside the inner scope so they outlive it. Allocate GM scratch just outside the `pl.at` that first writes it; inside `pl.at`, `pl.create_tensor` yields a tile. When measurement proves a ring is too small, pass `RunConfig(ring_task_window=..., ring_heap=..., ring_dep_pool=...)` with a scalar or four per-ring values. Initialize a runtime tensor with a kernel or `pl.full`; do not use the removed `init_value=` argument. Scopes are orchestration-only. `mode=AUTO` requires `auto_scope=False` on the enclosing function; `mode=MANUAL` is allowed in either mode. An AUTO scope may not nest inside a MANUAL scope, and `manual_scope` may not nest inside another `manual_scope`. `@pl.jit`, `@pl.jit.host`, and `@pl.jit.inline` accept `auto_scope=False`; `.incore` and `.opaque` reject it. Each accepts a scalar or exactly four per-ring values; 0 leaves the compile default. Sizing is per task, not process-global. Both L2 and L3 paths are documented to forward `RunConfig`; confirm the effective capacities from the metadata line rather than assuming the override landed. Inner scopes shorten intermediate lifetime and can reclaim memory earlier, but add scope bookkeeping and scheduling boundaries. Larger rings avoid deadlock and allow deeper in-flight work, but the static arena grows and can cause an `rtMalloc` OOM before the kernel runs. A scalar ring knob broadcasts, so one intended ring may enlarge all four; per-ring values avoid that. Splitting a scope reduces its peak but may duplicate work or expose more orchestration tensors. items.summary: `pl.read`/`pl.write` reach one element through the issuing core's data cache, and cache write-back happens in whole 64-byte lines. Concurrent task instances must own whole lines; disjoint element indices are not enough.
items.text: `pl.load`/`pl.store` move a tile by DMA. `pl.read`/`pl.write` move one element through the issuing core's data cache. A scalar write reaches DDR as a whole 64-byte cache line when the kernel ends, and different cores' caches are not kept coherent within a task. Two instances that write different elements in the same 64-byte line can each write back their own copy of all 64 bytes, so the last write-back wins and the other store disappears. The rule is that each instance must own whole 64-byte lines: 16 elements for INT32/FP32, 32 for FP16/BF16, 8 for INT64, and 64 for INT8. Within one instance there is no hazard because it runs sequentially on one core. The hazard applies to `pl.spmd(n)` with `n > 1` and to `for ... in pl.parallel(n)` instances the runtime may overlap. `ScalarWriteLineShared` warns when the compiler cannot prove whole-line ownership; it names the measured stride when it can analyze the index, and reports that a runtime index is unanalyzable otherwise. The warning is a question for a runtime index, not a verdict; if the layout invariant is real and documented, it can be disabled with `disabled_diagnostics`. Two different tasks writing one tensor are not reported, because their temporal overlap is unknown. A write guarded by `if blk == 0` is still reported conservatively because the check does not read predicates. Use `pl.spmd(1)` for a handful of control values, a per-instance scratch row for partial results, or `pl.store(..., atomic=pl.AtomicType.Add)` into a zero-initialized destination for a true cross-core scatter. Atomic-add order is not fixed, so floating-point results are non-deterministic. `pl.array.create(extent, dtype)` creates a small core-local array for cursors or TaskId fan-in; its extent must be compile-time constant, and updates are functional. A scalar read of a tensor is also legal in orchestration, where a device-computed count can become a host-side loop bound after casting to `pl.INDEX`. A scatter must be coherent across cores. Partition `pld`/tensor writes so each instance writes a contiguous run aligned to and sized in whole 64-byte lines. Use `pl.array.create(N, pl.INT32)` for a per-instance cursor and `pl.array.create(N, pl.TASK_ID)` for a TaskId fan-in. Cast a scalar read used as an offset or loop bound to `pl.INDEX`. Atomic-add destinations must be zero-initialized before the kernel. Supported atomic-add tile dtypes are fp32, bf16, fp16, int32, int16, and int8; bf16 atomic-add is documented for 910B/A2/A3 but not A5. A scalar loop over a tile-sized region is much slower than the corresponding vector op. `pl.write` returns an IR expression; the DSL parser surfaces it as an `EvalStmt`. `pl.array.create(extent, dtype)` supports integer, BOOL, or TASK_ID elements, requires a compile-time constant extent, is private to the creating block, and does not cross function boundaries. items.text: `scope_stats` writes one sample at every scope boundary: task-window, heap, dependency-pool head/tail, and tensormap usage. It works on both L2 and L3 paths; L2 writes under `dfx_outputs/scope_stats/`, L3 per rank and dispatch under `dfx_outputs/rank<N>/d<K>/scope_stats/`. Line 1 is run metadata carrying schema version, `fatal`, `dropped`, and the effective capacities `task_window_max`, `heap_max`, and `dep_pool_max` as arrays indexed by ring, plus `tensormap_max`. Every later line is a `begin` or `end` sample with a source `site`, depth, ring, and head/tail counters. In schema version 6 heap counters are monotonic cumulative bytes. Pair a begin with its end to compute `scope_high_water = end.head - begin.tail`, an upper bound on pressure reached; `real_occupancy = end.head - end.tail`, what is still held at exit; and `scope_alloc = end.head - begin.head`, allocation throughput independent of reclaim. A ring near capacity while others are near zero indicates auto-scope collapse or all work at one depth. High high-water with low live occupancy means the scope streams and reclaim keeps up. items.summary: `pl.pipeline(N, stage=F)` asks for ping-pong buffering. The default path replicates the body F times; under `memory_planner=PTOAS`, `LowerPipelineToSlots` may rotate one body through F slots of one allocation. Both paths have capacity and eligibility constraints, and explicit `pl.MemRef(..., slots=N)` is the hand-managed alternative.
items.text: `pl.pipeline(N, stage=F)` has the same positional shape as `pl.range` and requires a positive `stage`, typically 2 or 4. The default `LowerPipelineLoops` path replicates the body F times per outer iteration, advances the outer loop by `F * step`, and handles a remainder with a static tail or a dynamic cascaded `if`. Each clone gets fresh SSA def-vars, and tile-producing calls are tagged with `pipeline_membership(group, stage)` so `MemoryReuse` does not collapse concurrently live stage buffers. Only load buffers generally need per-stage privacy; giving every intermediate F copies overflows real kernels. The capacity gate chooses an affordable effective depth `F_g = min(depth_g, floor(C_s / slot_g))` and may shed groups. A `PH-MR-001` perf hint names the requested versus achieved depth and recommends shrinking the per-stage tile or lowering `stage=`. Under `memory_planner=PTOAS`, `LowerPipelineToSlots` runs before `LowerPipelineLoops` and can demote a safe loop to `pl.range` with one body whose load result is bound to `pl.MemRef('pipe_x', slots=F)[iv % F]`. This avoids a remainder dispatch and preserves one body. It is gated to F in [2,16], memory space Vec/Mat/Acc, a static valid shape, a tile not carried through a phi or view/in-place result, `step == 1`, `start % F == 0`, slots that fit the space, and no declined enclosing pipeline. The slot index must be literally `iv % F`; ptoas matches that affine form to derive per-slot synchronization. The declared slots are pinned, so the pass is accountable for their bytes and declines when the region would overflow. Explicit slots use `pl.MemRef('ub', slots=2)[i % 2]` inline in a tile annotation. Under the default PYPTO planner, two slots may co-live in one iteration; under PTOAS, two co-live slots in one iteration are rejected because only the first `multi_tile_get` is guarded. When a hand-managed rotation is required, write the `pl.MemRef('ub', slots=2)[i % 2]` declaration inline in the tile annotation, not through a Python variable holding the declaration. Under PTOAS, design each iteration to have one slot live at a time and keep `step == 1` with a start divisible by the stage. On `PH-MR-001`, shrink the per-stage tile to the stated byte budget or lower `stage=` instead of assuming the requested depth was achieved. `pl.pipeline` is InCore-only and requires `stage=N`; `stage=1` is a no-op marker that leaves the loop intact for IO canonicalization. items.summary: `allow_early_resolve=True` lets the scheduler pre-stage a consumer onto an idle core before its producer finishes, then release it with a doorbell. It works only when every direct producer is flagged or complete and the producer is fully published; it changes timing, not results.
items.text: The scheduler may pre-stage a not-yet-released task onto an idle core in a gated state. When its producers finish, a doorbell releases the already-staged payload, so pickup latency is removed from the critical path. The hint is producer-side and is accepted by `pl.at`, `pl.spmd`, `pl.submit`, and `pl.spmd_submit`. It is pure scheduling and does not affect results. Four conditions decide whether it does anything. First, every direct producer of the consumer must be flagged or already complete; flagging one producer of a three-producer consumer buys nothing. Second, a producer propagates eligibility only once it is fully published, meaning all its logical blocks have been published; this prevents a wave-dispatched SPMD producer from stranding later blocks. Third, normal work outranks early work, and the early lane is serviced only when normal lanes are empty; a saturated engine has no window to win. Fourth, a predicated task never early-dispatches, and a `sync_start` cohort needs all-or-nothing capacity, so it cannot itself be pre-staged block by block, though flagging it still lets its consumers pre-stage. `deps.json::tasks[].early_dispatch` records only that the task carries the producer-side flag; it is not proof that staging happened. items.text: `pl.spmd(core_num)` dispatches the same kernel over `core_num` blocks from one orchestrator schedule entry. The loop form is `for i in pl.spmd(n):`, where `i` is the per-block index and the body is auto-outlined into an InCore function. The context-manager form is `with pl.spmd(n):`; its body either dispatches a pre-defined InCore kernel or is an inline body that reads `pl.tile.get_block_idx()`. A body that neither reads the block index nor dispatches a kernel is rejected because every block would do identical work. Blocks are scheduled individually; with more blocks than cores the launch runs in waves unless `sync_start=True`, which forces an atomic all-or-nothing launch. For a hard `pl.system.syncall`, size the launch from the device with `pl.system.available_cluster_count()` for mixed or cube-only kernels and `pl.system.available_aiv_count()` for vector-only kernels, written inline at the call site, and set `sync_start=True`. Pass `optimizations=[pl.split(pl.SplitMode.UP_DOWN)]` only where cross-core splitting is intended; entries must be written inline. items.text: A task is one kernel dispatch. Its cost includes resolving dependencies, placing it on a compatible core, writing a dispatch descriptor, and observing completion. When tasks are very small, this administration can dominate the makespan and cores can sit idle even while ready work exists. The first remedy is to make each task larger: raise the tile shape so one task covers more elements. The second is to move a chunking loop inside the InCore region so one dispatch processes several chunks. The third is to merge adjacent `pl.at` regions so an intermediate stays on chip instead of round-tripping through GM. A mixed Cube+Vector merge is a special case: putting `pl.matmul` and its vector epilogue in one `pl.at` removes a hand-off, but a cross-engine merge needs a split mode; without one, the buffers may not fit and the compiler refuses the scope. A slice or load is never valid where the source is not: the source's valid region, shifted by the offset and cut to the window, bounds the result. `valid_shape` narrows; it cannot widen. A tensor slice with `clamp=True` sanctions a window that runs off the source and cuts the valid region to the source edge; a tile slice has no `clamp` because an on-chip window cannot overhang. `drop_dims` erases static unit axes from the result type; tile rank is clamped back to 2D. `pl.set_validshape(tile, valid_rows, valid_cols)` annotates an already-computed 2D tile when the valid extent is known only at runtime. items.text: `pl.Tensor` lives in DDR, `pl.Tile` is an on-chip buffer, `pl.Scalar` is a register-width value, `pl.Array` is a core-local array, and `pl.Tuple` is an annotation for multi-value returns. Shapes are static and checked at parse time. `pl.dynamic(name)` marks an axis whose extent is bound per launch; dynamic dimensions collapse to `None` in the JIT cache key, so one compiled program serves multiple extents, at the cost of compile-time shape knowledge. items.text:
This reference indexes the public source-level semantics for the compute domain.

- Cube Matmul, Accumulator Predicates, and L0C Windows: `pl.matmul`, `pl.matmul_acc`, and `pl.matmul_bias` map to the Cube unit; `pl.gemv*` specialize M=1. Float accumulates in FP32 and INT8 in INT32. `init_cond` removes the peeled first K step, but rank and L0C-window rules have unresolved or strict cases.
- Gather, Scatter, and Sort Contracts: Gather and scatter have index and mask forms with different rank, index-width, and destination-stride rules. Sort/top-k is single-row: `sort32` produces interleaved value-index runs and `mrgsort` merges them using a block length measured in interleaved positions.
- Ascend 220x Alignment, Cache, and Unit Constraints: On the local CANN 9.0.0 implementation for 910B4/C220, FixPipe has operand-specific address units: ReluPre uses a 64-byte FPC field while QuantPre/dequant FBUF uses a 128-byte FPC field and transfer unit. Do not collapse these into one universal FixPipe alignment rule.
- Rounding Modes, Dtype Alignment, and Quantization Precision: Most apparent kernel errors are avoidable precision losses: the wrong cast rounding mode, a dtype that silently widened or narrowed, a two-hop cast, or a golden that computes a different order. Keep intermediates in the widest free type, cast once at the consuming boundary, and align kernel, golden, and stored weights.
- Reduction and Broadcast Operation Contracts: Row and column reductions collapse different axes and have different scratch-tile contracts on tensor versus tile APIs. Broadcast expansions are single hardware ops, comparison masks need `sel` scratch, and precision flags are operation-specific.
- Types, Dynamic Shapes, Directions, and Layout Contracts: A PyPTO type says where a value lives, how wide its elements are, and how callers may touch it. Shapes are static by default; dynamic axes trade planning information for reuse. Parameter direction and layout are semantic inputs to dependency inference and matmul lowering, not documentation.

items.summary: Memory API and mechanism index
items.text:
This reference indexes the public source-level semantics for the memory domain.

- Cache Policy, Streaming Reads, and L2 Residency Warming: `pl.set_cache_policy(tensor, pl.CachePolicy.BYPASS)` declares every read of a tensor in a scope streaming; `pl.load(..., cache=...)` declares one access. BYPASS is a coherence and no-reuse contract, not a hint. The installed toolchain has no L2-bypass path yet, so it warns and compiles as an ordinary cached access.
- Cube Tile Sizing Against Mat, Acc, Vec, and the 512-Byte Line: Choose M, N, and K by ranking shapes, rejecting them against the compiler's Mat/Acc/Vec report, then measuring survivors. Growing N or K increases the L1 weight fragment; growing M or N increases the L0C accumulator; a K-contiguous transfer below the cache-line floor can lose more than a wider N gains.
- Address Allocation, DSA-RP, and Cross-Core Reserve Buffers: `AllocateMemoryAddr` gives concrete addresses to non-DDR MemRefs. PYPTO uses deterministic 32-byte-aligned sequential allocation per space; DSA_RP solves capacity-constrained placement with reuse penalties; PTOAS skips the pass. `pl.reserve_buffer` and cross-core pipe rings can dominate an overflow.
- Memory Hierarchy and Legal Data Movement: DDR, Vec, Mat, Left, Right, Acc, and Bias are separate buffers, not nested regions. A DDR-facing load can land only in Vec or Mat; specialized matmul spaces are reached by `pl.move` or written by `pl.matmul`.
- Opportunistic Memory Reuse and Author-Declared Allocations: `MemoryReuse` coalesces tiles with non-overlapping lifetimes in the same space, subject to no-alias constraints and a pipeline-stage capacity guard. Author-declared `pl.MemRef` allocations are pinned and isolated; they trade capacity for scheduling independence and have planner-specific restrictions.
- Runtime Scopes, Ring Heaps, and Intermediate Lifetime: A runtime scope is both a dependency-tracking boundary and a heap tier. Four ring sets are selected by scope nesting depth, so placing scopes changes when intermediate GM tensors are reclaimed. Memory is freed at scope exit and FIFO reclaim, not at last use.
- Scalar Access and the 64-Byte Write Granularity: `pl.read`/`pl.write` reach one element through the issuing core's data cache, and cache write-back happens in whole 64-byte lines. Concurrent task instances must own whole lines; disjoint element indices are not enough.
- Scope Stats and Ring Deadlock Diagnosis: `enable_scope_stats` records task-window, heap, dependency-pool, and tensormap usage at every scope boundary. The first JSONL line proves effective ring capacities; paired begin/end samples show high-water, live occupancy, and allocation throughput, while `orch_error_code` names the resource that wedged.
- Slicing, Valid Shapes, Padding, and Shape Views: A tile has an allocated shape and an optional valid region. Loads and slices only read source bytes that exist, reductions see the padding, and `fillpad`/`set_validshape` make the tail explicit. Argument order and view restrictions differ between `pl.slice`, `pl.load`, and `pl.store`.
